title: Ali Fazal Just Made the Most Disturbing Show on Indian OTT. You Won't Be Able to Look Away.
excerpt: Based on the real Ranga-Billa kidnapping that shook 1978 Delhi, Raakh on Prime Video is eight episodes of dread, grief, and forensic fury — with Sonali Bendre's most devastating performance in years.
body:
The opening scene of **Raakh** is deceptively quiet. Two siblings — **Suman**, sixteen, and **Sahil**, fourteen — leave their Delhi Cantonment home on a rain-soaked evening. She's headed to a radio station to sing on air. He tags along because that's what little brothers do. Their parents tune in, expecting to hear their daughter's voice. Someone else sings instead. The children never come home.

What follows across eight episodes is one of the most unsettling, meticulously crafted pieces of Indian crime television since *Delhi Crime*. Now streaming on **Amazon Prime Video**, **Raakh** is a fictionalized account of the infamous **Ranga-Billa case of 1978** — the kidnapping and brutal murder of siblings Geeta and Sanjay Chopra that paralyzed Delhi and eventually led to one of independent India's most publicized manhunts and hangings.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=RdB_TgwLPqs</youtube>


Directed by **Prosit Roy** — the man behind *Paatal Lok* — the series turns what could have been a standard procedural into something closer to a slow-burning horror film. The Hollywood Reporter India called it "suffocating, immersive, and terrifying." They're not wrong.

https://www.instagram.com/p/DZdFU2FjgH3/

## Guddu Bhaiya Goes Dark

**Ali Fazal** plays SI Jayprakash Jatav, the young officer thrown headfirst into the investigation. If you know him as Guddu from *Mirzapur* — chaotic, emotional, trigger-happy — forget all of it. Here, Fazal is restrained to the point of combustion. He's a rookie cop with a complicated relationship with his father (played by **Rakesh Bedi**, in a casting choice that works far better than it should), navigating a case that breaks him open in ways the show is smart enough to let you feel rather than explain.

The performance is a career recalibration. Fazal has always been good — *Death on the Nile*, *Victoria & Abdul*, *Mirzapur* — but Raakh asks him to do something harder than intensity: it asks him to be still. And in that stillness, you see a cop who knows he's losing a race against time.

**Sonali Bendre** returns to the screen as Mona Arora, the children's mother, and her performance is devastating. This is Bendre's most substantial role in years, and she inhabits it with a grief so raw that certain scenes play almost like documentary footage. Opposite her, **Aamir Bashir** as the ex-army father brings a military stoicism that cracks, incrementally, until it doesn't hold anymore.

## The Villains You'll Despise

The show's biggest revelation belongs to the killers. **Akash Makhija** and **Ramandeep Yadav** play Babu and Rajjo — the fictional stand-ins for Ranga and Billa — with a complete absence of redemption. Critics have called their performances "horrifyingly believable," and it's accurate. There is no tragic backstory that earns your sympathy. There is no moment where you glimpse their humanity. They derive a high from what they're doing, and the parallel timeline — intercutting the investigation with their escalating violence in the days before the kidnapping — is narratively risky but devastating.

> The cat-and-mouse chase may frustrate some viewers. These are people operating without modern technology, relying entirely on instinct, contacts, intelligence, and persistence. But that frustration is precisely the point.

The series also quietly charts the birth of modern forensic investigation in India. Initially mocked even by Jayprakash himself, the forensic department gradually proves its value — a detail that enriches the storytelling without ever feeling like a lecture.

## Why the Diaspora Should Watch This

For NRIs, the Ranga-Billa case occupies a specific, haunting space in cultural memory. If your parents grew up in Delhi in the '70s, they remember it. It was the case that changed how Indian families thought about safety — the moment when accepting a lift from a stranger stopped being ordinary and became something parents warned you about for decades.

**Raakh** understands this. It's not just a crime show. It's a period piece about a city learning what urban fear feels like. The production design is immaculate — every frame feels authentically 1978, from the Fiat cars to the radio station interiors. The cinematography by **Saumyananda Sahi** and the sound design by **Anish John** keep you in a state of near-constant dread.

At eight episodes, Raakh doesn't overstay its welcome. It's taut, disturbing, beautifully acted, and constructed with a precision that most Indian OTT shows don't bother attempting. India Forums declared it "the year's best show." Bollywood Hungama called it "hard-hitting and disturbing." MensXP said it proves "there is still novelty left in the genre."

If you have Prime Video — and if you're reading this from the US, UK, or Canada, you almost certainly do — this is what your weekend should look like.

**All eight episodes of Raakh are streaming now on Amazon Prime Video.**
